lede: 219 packages in one repo, every one of them carrying a slot for a "runtime self-check" — not a single gap. Sounds like the discipline landed. But ask the next question — does any of this actually run in production? — and the answer is: not one of them. Two places in the entire repo hook it into a running system: the unit-test bootstrap, and one example assembly. The interesting part isn't that this is an oversight. It's that it isn't one at all. **Every rule a script can check, this repo enforces at 100%. Every rule a script can't check falls back entirely to good intentions. Almost all of this architecture's costs grow along that line.**

sections.heading: A self-check system, fully installed, never plugged in
body: Making every module declare what relationships it maintains at runtime is a good idea. A line in the docs saying "this module guarantees the queue is never consumed twice" is just a sentence. Turn it into an assertion that runs at startup and it becomes something executable.
The hard part was never writing the assertion. It's getting it to happen evenly. Across two hundred-odd packages, good intentions always leave gaps.
The usual move is to write it into the conventions and let review catch the misses. This repo went harder: it made the thing a gate.

The gate checks four things — does the package have the file, does the manifest export it, is the dependency declared, is the compiler config wired up. All four can be decided mechanically from file contents, so the pass rate is 100%. Not one package missing.

Then you open those 219 files and read them: 184 are empty. The body does nothing, with a comment above it explaining why this package has no runtime relationship worth asserting. The ones that actually check something: 35.

Worse is the registry responsible for hooking those assertions into a running system. Two places in the whole repo mount it: the global setup for unit tests, and one example assembly — and that one pulls in only four companion plugins. None of the three shipped profiles has it, and neither does any config file.
In other words, what this thing really is, is a test-time assertion library. Not a production self-check.
And every package manifest declares a dependency on it in black and white — because the gate demands it — so the fact that it's never actually mounted is invisible from the dependency relationships.
**A gap opens between the structure being complete and the behavior being live, and both sides of that gap look identical.**

sections.heading: Machine-generated, but only one column is guaranteed
body: At the top of the doc: generated by a script, do not edit by hand. A reader who sees that line assumes the whole page is machine-guaranteed.
That's a reasonable assumption. And it's exactly that assumption that makes what follows dangerous.

This document is one of the most important indexes in the repo: 26 capability seams, each listed with three columns — the package that owns the interface, the packages known to implement it, the packages that consume it directly.

The script does generate something — it scans the underlying framework's service declarations and produces the list of services. But those three columns come from a hand-typed array in the script's own source, entered row by row.

There is a completeness check, and it runs both ways: scanned but not entered is an error, entered but not scanned is an error too. It just only compares the key. The implementer column and the consumer column are never looked at, start to finish.
At render time, each package's short name is looked up in an index. A hit renders as a repo link. A miss — it prints verbatim as a code literal. No error, no warning, no count.
Visually, the two differ by an underline.

13 names in that table took this path. Five have no corresponding package in the repo at all. The other eight are typos in the short name, and one of them fails in a particularly telling way: another row of the same table links correctly to the same package.
**This isn't a stale doc — it's the word "generated" being stretched too far. One column is actually machine-guaranteed; the banner vouches for the whole page.**

sections.heading: Half the seams have exactly one implementation
body: The repo's core organizing principle is the capability seam: a capability splits into three roles — the one defining the interface, the one providing an implementation, the one using it — each in its own package. The rule is stated plainly: a seam arrives as a complete set, never as one role alone.
That rule solves a real problem. If a capability will have several implementations and you don't define the interface first, the second implementation forces you to touch every caller.
The trouble is it only says how to build one. It never says when not to.

Of the 26 seams, 15 have zero or one implementation. The zero is "ask the user a question," whose implementation is registered at runtime by the UI front end. The ones with exactly one: settings, credentials, sandboxing, compaction, background jobs, terminals, the workflow engine, language services, code runtimes, session queries, session telemetry, attachments, overflow storage.
Genuinely multi-implementation seams are the minority:
- subagents, 6 implementations
- web capability, 4
- model adapters, command execution, filesystem — 3 each
Those were forced out by real demand: different model vendors, different sandbox worlds, different transports for subagents.

The cost of a single-implementation seam isn't at runtime — at runtime it's one layer of direct calls. The cost is the fixed overhead of reading and maintaining it: at least three packages per seam, each with its own manifest, docs, compiler config, test directory, and that forever-empty invariant slot.
A sizeable share of that 219 came from exactly this.
**The missing half of the rule — when not to open a seam — is precisely where speculative abstraction gets in. The abstraction isn't the mistake. The timing is.**

sections.heading: The exceptions all pile up in the same corner
body: How well a set of design rules is enforced isn't something averages tell you. Look at where the exceptions land.
In this repo they're almost all crowded into one area: the browser front end, and the host gateway sitting behind it.

The gateway's main implementation is a single 3,744-line file, second largest in the repo, in a package that directly depends on 28 others. Inside is one plugin body holding dozens of closures that handle sessions, workspaces, targets, settings, presets, model routing, projections, attachments, and asking the user questions.

It registers no seam of its own. In the seam table its service is marked core, with zero implementations and one consumer. Everywhere else the pattern is one capability split across three layers. Here it's one function consuming 28 packages — the arrow points the other way.

The coverage gate springs its leak here too. The gate itself is set hard: scored per file, 100% on statements, branches, functions, and lines. One file short by one line turns the whole thing red, and high coverage elsewhere can't make it up.
But a hard gate didn't make the code more testable. It only made the exclusion list the sole relief valve. Of 1,316 source files, 260 are excluded — 26% by physical line count.

And what's excluded isn't scattered edge cases: the entire "let the agent modify its own runtime" capability, 16,134 lines, wiped out by one wildcard; three of the gateway's files named individually; dozens of browser-side files listed one by one.

The list also has a comment pointing at a package group that was renamed long ago. That wildcard matches zero files and raises no error — the intent behind it happens to be covered by the line right next to it, so nobody noticed.

The dependency graph goes blind in the same place. A manifest can declare a dependency two ways, and the graph's data source reads only one of them: 1,089 edges go in, and another 205 written in the other field are never looked at.

Add those back and a four-node cycle appears immediately — the browser-side connection layer depends on the host gateway, the gateway depends on the remote service descriptions, the descriptions depend on the call gateway, and the call gateway depends back on the connection layer. The generator has a topological sort and it has cycle detection. By construction, it cannot see this cycle.

**How evenly a rule is enforced tells you more than how strict the rule is. And exceptions never scatter randomly — they cluster in one area, and that area is where the design hasn't actually reached yet.**

sections.heading: Fail loud lives at the door, silent skip lives inside
body: One of the repo's rules is written very hard: misconfiguration fails loud, anything decidable at load time throws at load time, and a reference that can't be found is never silently skipped.
The patch layer doesn't follow it.

The patch layer is a good design in itself: to change one plugin's config you don't touch the base config, you write a line saying find this marker and replace it with this. Multiple sources stack in layers — one per shipped profile, one for the user, one more from the command line.

The hard part is that layered stacking naturally tolerates "the line I'm referring to hasn't been inserted yet." An upper layer may not have run at all while a lower one references it, and throwing on every such case would make the whole layering scheme extremely brittle.

So it chose leniency: four kinds of match failure — target not found, target isn't a group, a non-insert patch with no marker, a declared name that doesn't match the target — all warn and skip. The whole patch is dropped and the process continues.
The problem is the warning itself.

On the runtime path, the warning goes into a logging service fetched through an optional chain: no logging plugin mounted, nothing happens. The offline-composition entry point is more direct still — the warning parameter defaults to an empty function, and no caller in the repo has ever passed a real one. There's even a test pinning down the behavior "returns an empty list when the target doesn't exist."
Net effect: misspell one letter of a plugin marker in your own patch file and you get a completely silent no-op. Nothing happens, and nobody tells you nothing happened.

The contrast makes it clearer: in the same layer, "the patch file exists but won't parse" does throw. **Loud at the file level, silent at the entry level — a rule written in the docs and a throw wired into the outermost layer don't mean the inner layers do the same.**

sections.heading: How a repo describes itself
body: The last category of cost isn't in the code. It's in how this repo describes itself.

The docs present one event dispatch mode as this repo's extension mechanism: a listener gets a "keep going" handle, calling it passes control to the next layer, not calling it short-circuits the chain.

That's textbook onion middleware. And it's one of five dispatch modes that ship with the upstream framework copied in alongside the repo, sitting next to the other four. It came from upstream. It wasn't invented here.
Same with capability seams. Interface, implementation, consumer is the standard split from ports and adapters — hexagonal architecture — under a different name.

Renaming isn't wrong in itself, and it genuinely lowers the cost of talking about this stuff inside the team. The problem is that the docs present it as a design characteristic of this repo, so readers overestimate how novel any of it is.

And nothing gates the three-role structure. The repo has dozens of verification scripts covering comment completeness, doc word budgets, package paths, workspace constraints, diagram syntax, translation pairing, licenses — not one of them checks whether a seam has all three of its roles. The two scripts that mention seam roles at all are both doc generators.

One piece of self-description has already expired. The repo's top-level doc carries an interim clause premised on "no external consumers yet," which on that basis authorizes free renaming and repackaging, and states plainly: remove this section at the first tagged release.
The repo now has three tags, all 219 packages are configured for public publishing, and none is marked private. The condition was met a while ago.
That section is still there, still in force. **Nothing alerts anyone the moment a tag appears — because this rule was written for people to read, not for a script.**

mechanisms.name: Somebody owns the slot, nobody owns plugging it in
mechanisms.how: The usual approach is to write "every module declares its runtime invariants" into the conventions and let review nag. Here it was made a gate: does the file exist, does the manifest export it, is the dependency declared, is the compiler config wired — four things decidable mechanically from file contents, so all 219 packages pass and none is missing. But whether the service that hooks those assertions into a running system ever gets mounted into a runtime context is an assembly-time decision, outside the view of any static gate, and nothing else covers it.
mechanisms.why: A gate can only check what it can read. Treating "the file exists" as evidence that "the mechanism runs" is the most common way this kind of gap opens.

mechanisms.name: The check compares only the key column
mechanisms.how: The usual approach is that a generator is either fully automatic or fully hand-written, and readers judge its trustworthiness accordingly. Here it's mixed: the service list is scanned out of the framework's declarations, while the owner, implementer, and consumer columns are a hand-typed array. The validation takes a two-way difference between the scan and the array — scanned but not entered is an error, entered but not scanned is an error — but it compares only the key. The other two columns are never examined. So the key stays perpetually fresh while the associated data is free to rot without tripping a single signal.
mechanisms.why: The check covers the column most likely to drift, which makes it that much easier to believe the whole table is covered.

mechanisms.name: A miss quietly degrades
mechanisms.how: The usual approach is to throw on a lookup miss so the problem surfaces the moment the doc is generated. Here the fallback is: a hit renders as a link, a miss wraps the original string in backticks and prints it as a code literal — no error, no warning, no count. In a 26-row table where each row carries a dozen or more names, a link and a code literal differ visually by an underline. 13 names took this fallback path, and 5 of them name packages that don't exist in the repo at all.
mechanisms.why: Rendering a miss as valid output is how an error gets to look like a correct one.

mechanisms.name: The graph sees only half the edges
mechanisms.how: The usual approach is for a dependency graph to read every dependency field in the manifest. Here it reads one of them — by repo convention, package-to-package relationships are supposed to use that one anyway. 1,089 edges go into the graph; another 205 written elsewhere are ignored entirely. The gap between the convention and reality is exactly what the tool is blind to: add the 205 back and a four-node cycle appears at once among the browser connection layer, the host gateway, the remote descriptions, and the call gateway. The same script has cycle detection. It's just that the graph it sorts doesn't contain this cycle.
mechanisms.why: What a tool takes as input decides what it can find. A graph that looks clean only means it wasn't looking at that part.

mechanisms.name: A hard gate just relocates the untested code
mechanisms.how: The usual approach is a single overall coverage percentage, where easy-to-test files carry the hard ones. Here it's scored per file, all four metrics at 100%, one file short by one line turns everything red, and nothing elsewhere can compensate. At that intensity the exclusion list becomes the only workable relief valve — hard-to-test files aren't held to a lower bar, they're moved out of the measurement entirely. The list currently drops 260 files, 26% of physical lines. Entries are wildcard strings, and a mistyped path that matches zero files raises no error either.
mechanisms.why: The hard gate didn't eliminate untested code. It moved it from the coverage report into a config file.

mechanisms.name: Only what can be scripted gets enforced
mechanisms.how: The usual approach is to write design rules into docs and enforce them at review. This repo goes further and turns everything mechanically decidable into a script: does an export have a comment, is a doc over its word budget, is a package path legal, are the doc links dead, are the translation files paired. What's left — whether a seam has all three roles, whether a seam with one implementation should exist at all, whether a 3,744-line file should be split — needs human judgment, so all of it falls back to code review.
mechanisms.why: This explains the shape shared by every cost catalogued here: the scriptable part sits near 100%, and the unscriptable part depends on how much attention the reviewer had that day.

lessons.lesson: Score structural checks and behavioral checks separately.
lessons.why: All 219 packages have the slot, declare the dependency correctly, and pass the gate — and not one assertion runs in a production assembly. Statically checkable facts are easy to get to 100%, which is exactly why they get mistaken for evidence that the mechanism works. The question to ask is who mounts it at runtime, not whether the file exists.

lessons.lesson: A generated doc must validate every column it renders, and throw on a lookup miss.
lessons.why: A generator that validates only the key creates the impression of a machine guarantee while the associated columns rot freely. Worse is the silent degrade to plain text on a miss — the error gets rendered as valid output. Either validate it, or stop generating the moment something won't resolve.

lessons.lesson: Wait until the second implementation actually exists before opening a seam.
lessons.why: 15 of 26 seams have zero or one implementation, and each still pays the fixed cost of at least three packages. The multi-implementation ones do earn their keep, which shows the abstraction isn't the mistake — the timing is. The test is that the second implementation already exists, not that you can picture it existing.

lessons.lesson: Wire "fail loud" into the innermost layer, not just a throw at the outermost.
lessons.why: A patch file that won't parse throws; a patch entry that matches nothing only warns and skips. And that warning goes through a logging service fetched by optional chain, so with no logger mounted it's completely silent. A rule in the docs and a throw on the outside don't mean the inside does the same — misspell one letter and you get a fully silent no-op.

lessons.lesson: A self-deletion condition written into the docs needs someone checking on a schedule whether it has come due.
lessons.why: That interim clause is premised on having no external consumers, authorizes free renaming and repackaging, and says to remove the section at the first tagged release. Three tags exist, all 219 packages are configured for public publishing, the condition has long been met — and nothing alerts anyone when a tag appears.

tradeoffs: The empty slots aren't worth nothing: 184 comments saying "this package has no runtime invariant" are written conclusions from authors who were forced to answer what runtime relationship their package actually maintains — better than the default silence you get with no slot at all. And at test time all 35 real assertions do get mounted and executed.

A few seams counted as single-implementation aren't speculative at all: sandboxing is three completely different implementation paths across three operating systems, the filesystem already has three implementations, and subprocesses have two — local and remote sandbox. Lumping those in with speculative abstraction isn't fair.

Those three hand-written role columns genuinely resist automatic derivation: a package "implementing" a service shows up in this framework as one registration call at runtime, and static analysis would have to trace calls like that across packages. Hand-writing them plus a key check is a clear-eyed read on what automation would cost. It's just that the banner's wording doesn't reflect the trade.

The host gateway is the browser front end's only backend entry point, and a large share of those 3,744 lines is one-to-one translation of internal services into wire calls. Forcing that kind of code into separate packages would add seams without removing code. And being excluded from coverage isn't the same as being untested — protocol-parity tests and end-to-end snapshots still pin down its external behavior.

Nearly every entry in the coverage exclusion list carries a TODO marker and an exit condition ("cover and remove once the browser-side test channel matures"), which is bookkeeping, not concealment. The 26% concentrates in GUI code and code generators, two categories that have always been hard to test, rather than scattering randomly through business logic.

The patch layer's leniency has a legitimate source: when layers stack, one layer referencing a line another layer may not have inserted is normal, and throwing on all of it would make the composition brittle. What actually needs fixing is that the layer a user hand-writes and the layers between shipped profiles share the same leniency policy.
